title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
A transcription service recorded virtual meetings by default without notifying all participants that their conversations would be used to train its AI systems. The service operated across Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams, reaching approximately 25 million users. The lawsuit alleges that consent was buried in account setup procedures, leaving many users unaware their words would be fed into machine learning systems.

The failure happened at the deployment stage, where default settings enabled recording and data collection without affirmative consent from all meeting participants. This is a case of a system trained on data collected without adequate notification or permission from those whose speech was captured. It would have taken either explicit opt-in consent from all participants before recording, or explicit notification to all participants at the time recording began, to prevent this class of harm.

It is not established whether the company's de-identification process was adequate, whether the privacy policy language was sufficient as a legal matter, or whether the allegations in the lawsuit will be proven in court.

Enterprise note-taking apps face legal scrutiny as Otter hit with privacy suit

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed against Otter.ai, a Mountain View-based artificial intelligence company, alleges the firm secretly records private work conversations without consent to train its transcription service. The suit, filed by California resident Justin Brewer, claims Otter's meeting recording software records virtual meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams by default without notifying all participants that their conversations will be shared with Otter to improve its AI systems. The company serves approximately 25 million users who have recorded over 1 billion meetings since 2016.

The lawsuit contends that Otter violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws through its deceptive practices. While Otter's privacy policy mentions users grant permission when checking a box during account setup, the suit maintains many people are still unaware their conversations are being used for AI training. Recent controversies include reports that Otter recorded sensitive investor meetings and conversations with human rights activists without proper consent. Otter claims it de-identifies audio before feeding it into its machine learning systems, though the lawsuit questions whether this process adequately removes confidential information.
